san3: How many times can you stand up from a chair in 30 seconds? This simple test measures the strength and endurance of your legs. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) uses it to assess fall risk in older adults. Your phone’s camera can count your repetitions for you; the video never leaves your device.

san78: Only full stands count. If you are more than halfway up when the time runs out, that stand also counts. If you need to use your arms to stand up, the test stops and the result is 0.
san79: The CDC recommends that someone stands next to you during the test. If you have fallen recently, feel dizzy or have balance problems, do not do the test alone.

san88: The test itself is its best exercise. On a sturdy chair without armrests, with your arms crossed over your chest, stand up and sit down at a controlled pace. If this is too hard, start by pushing up with your arms or by using a higher chair.

san96: Is my camera image sent anywhere?
san97: No. The image is processed only on your own device, inside your browser; it is not recorded or sent to any server. The first time you turn on the camera, the motion detection software (Google’s open-source MediaPipe model, about 17 MB in total) is downloaded to your device; all the counting happens on your device. Your results are also stored only on this device.
san98: What if the camera counts wrongly?
san99: The camera counter is a helper, not a perfect one. Loose clothing, poor light or your legs moving out of view can upset the count. When the test ends, you can correct the number yourself. The most reliable way is for someone next to you to count as well.
san100: What if I can’t stand up without using my arms?
san101: Under the CDC’s STEADI protocol, if you need to use your arms to stand up, the test is stopped and the result is recorded as 0. This shows that your leg strength needs support; it would be a good idea to have an assessment with a physiotherapist or doctor.
san103: Yes. Leg strength can improve with exercise at any age. You can start with the exercises below and repeat the test every few weeks to follow your progress. In a study of people with hip osteoarthritis, an increase of 2 stands was considered a meaningful improvement.
